# Diseño del programa · kurasu (feedback de una sesión)

Repositorio: este repositorio (`/home/agus/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course`), con el monorepo de kurasu en `app/`, en `main` y sin cambios sin commitear. Cubre las seis ramas de `../design.md` y la nota `app/docs/architecture/feedback-de-sesion.md` con las notas que actualizó (commit `9f078a3`). Deja afuera los casos de prueba y las validaciones manuales (`mahou:test-design`).

Fuente: `../design.md`, `app/docs/architecture/feedback-de-sesion.md`, `../prototypes/feedback.html` y `../prototypes/teacher-feedback.html`.

## Árbol

```
Program design · feedback de una sesión
└─ kurasu (app/)                                                                                         open
   ├─ 1 POST /admin/polls · el tipo feedback                                                             settled
   │  ✓ PollType suma "feedback" en el contract y en el enum de la columna (design.md, rama 1)
   │  ✓ Sin migración: la columna type es text sin CHECK y el snapshot no guarda el enum (sigue de 0003_changelog_and_ids)
   │  ✓ fitsType no cambia: el feedback no lleva opciones ni textos de escala, igual que la word cloud (sigue de fits-type.ts)
   │  ✓ ResponseValue suma { pick: 1..5, text?: string } (design.md, rama 1)
   │  ✓ PollResults suma feedback: cinco conteos, uno por punto (sigue de una clave por tipo en PollResults)
   ├─ 2 PATCH /polls/:id · la respuesta del alumno                                                       settled
   │  ✓ fitsPoll acepta en una encuesta de feedback solo un valor con pick (design.md, rama 3)
   │  ✓ Polls.vote guarda el valor sin la clave text cuando text llega vacío (feedback-de-sesion.md, "puede ir vacío o faltar")
   │  ✓ La encuesta de feedback vuelve con results null, abierta o cerrada (decisiones D13)
   │  ✓ El upsert por (pollId, userId) ya reemplaza la respuesta anterior y conserva su id (sigue de Polls.vote)
   ├─ 3 GET /admin/polls · el resumen del profe                                                          settled
   │  ✓ tally cuenta los pick en cinco barras (design.md, rama 5)
   │  ✓ La query de conteos agrupa una respuesta de feedback por su pick, sin el texto (acceso-a-datos.md)
   ├─ 4 GET /admin/responses · la lista del profe                                                        open
   │  ✓ Recurso nuevo /api/admin/responses con ?pollId=, no anidado en la encuesta (wiki api)
   │  ✓ Cada fila trae id, user { id, name, avatar }, pick y text cuando hay (sigue de RaisedHand)
   │  ✓ Ordenada por el id de la respuesta (design.md, rama 5, Q3)
   │  ✓ Polls.listFeedback lee la encuesta y ResponsesStore.feedbackOf hace la query con users (sigue de D1Hands.raisedIn)
   │  ❔ Q1 · Qué responde para una encuesta que no es de feedback
   │  ❔ Q2 · Cuántas filas devuelve
   ├─ 5 Tarjeta de feedback del alumno · inicio y aula                                                   settled
   │  ✓ Seis estados de prototypes/feedback.html (design.md, rama 4)
   │  ✓ VoteForm le pasa la encuesta de feedback a FeedbackForm, así ActivePolls, StudentPollsTab y el skeleton del aula no cambian (sigue de VoteForm.tsx, que ya separa la word cloud)
   │  ✓ FeedbackAnswer muestra la respuesta en el estado de gracias y en la encuesta cerrada (prototypes/feedback.html)
   │  ✓ ClosedPolls pone FeedbackAnswer en el cuerpo de un feedback cerrado, porque no tiene resultados (sigue de D13)
   │  ✓ PollCard elige el ícono por tipo: chat-messages para el feedback (prototypes/feedback.html)
   │  ✓ pollMeta dice "Encuesta de feedback · se puede cambiar" o "· cerrada" (prototypes/feedback.html)
   │  ✓ El error es inline en la tarjeta y sin toast, como la word cloud (prototypes/feedback.html y wiki web)
   │  ✓ La web no manda text cuando el campo está vacío (design.md, rama 1)
   ├─ 6 Tarjeta de feedback del profe · pestaña Encuestas                                                settled
   │  ✓ NewPollMenu suma "Feedback" y el editor muestra solo la pregunta (prototypes/teacher-feedback.html)
   │  ✓ PollResults suma la rama feedback: las barras de la escala con el emoji debajo y tres textos de extremos (design.md, rama 5)
   │  ✓ "Ver las respuestas" va primero entre las acciones, por un slot nuevo de PollActions (prototypes/teacher-feedback.html)
   │  ✓ La lista se abre en un Sheet titulado con el total de respuestas (prototypes/teacher-feedback.html)
   │  ✓ El panel del aula muestra las barras y no la lista (sigue de PanelPollCard, que solo activa y cierra)
   │  ✓ La lista se pide al abrir el Sheet y se vuelve a pedir con cada aviso de encuestas del aula (wiki web, useClassroom)
   └─ 7 Standards                                                                                        pending
```

## Lo que el diseño deja para el programa

- La forma de la rama de feedback en `ResponseValue` y la de su conteo en `PollResults`.
- Si hace falta migración para el tipo nuevo.
- Dónde se saca el texto vacío y dónde se niegan los resultados al alumno.
- Cómo la query de conteos cuenta los puntos sin leer los textos.
- El endpoint de la lista con nombres: su ruta, su forma, su orden, su tope y qué responde para otro tipo de encuesta.
- En qué componentes entra la tarjeta del alumno sin tocar a cada pantalla que muestra encuestas.
- Dónde va "Ver las respuestas", qué pieza abre la lista y cómo se refresca.

---

## 1 POST /admin/polls · el tipo feedback

Parte que se saltea: el callstack, porque crear una encuesta de feedback recorre el mismo camino que una word cloud y solo cambia el literal del tipo. La rama es el modelo compartido que usan las demás.

### 1.1 Class diagram · settled

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class PollType:::changed {
        +"choice" | "words" | "scale" | "feedback"
        <<Schema.Literals, contract>>
    }
    class FeedbackValue:::added {
        +number pick
        +string text
        <<rama de ResponseValue; pick entero 1 a 5; text optionalKey, sin tope>>
    }
    class PollResults:::changed {
        +number[] feedback
        <<optionalKey, cinco enteros como scale>>
    }
    class polls_type:::changed {
        +text type
        <<enum de drizzle solo en TS, sin CHECK, sin migración>>
    }
```

`FeedbackValue` es la cuarta rama de la unión `ResponseValue` (`packages/contract/src/polls.ts:63`), al lado de `choice`, `scale` y `words`. Como las otras ramas, es un `Schema.Struct` sin clave de tipo: la rama se reconoce por la presencia de `pick`. `text` es `Schema.optionalKey(Schema.String)`, así que una respuesta sin texto no lleva la clave y una con texto vacío decodifica y llega al core, que la saca (2.3).

`PollResults.feedback` sigue a `PollResults.scale`: cinco enteros, uno por punto. La columna `polls.type` es `text` sin `CHECK` desde `0003_changelog_and_ids/migration.sql:74` y el snapshot de drizzle no guarda el enum, así que sumar el literal en `schema.ts:85` no genera migración. Los `decode` de `D1Polls` y `D1Responses` usan los mismos schemas del contract, así que leen el tipo y la rama nuevos sin cambios propios.

### 1.2 Interfaces y module list · settled

```json
{
  "title": "PollType",
  "$comment": "exists",
  "enum": ["choice", "words", "scale", "feedback"],
  "description": "El tipo de la encuesta; feedback se suma al final."
}
```

```json
{
  "title": "ResponseValue",
  "$comment": "exists",
  "oneOf": [
    { "$comment": "unchanged", "title": "choice" },
    { "$comment": "unchanged", "title": "scale" },
    { "$comment": "unchanged", "title": "words" },
    {
      "$comment": "added",
      "title": "feedback",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "pick": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 5, "description": "El emoji elegido, como número de 1 a 5." },
        "text": { "type": "string", "description": "El comentario, tal como lo escribió. Ausente cuando no escribió nada." }
      },
      "required": ["pick"]
    }
  ]
}
```

```json
{
  "title": "PollResults",
  "$comment": "exists",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "feedback": { "$comment": "added", "type": "array", "items": { "type": "integer" }, "minItems": 5, "maxItems": 5, "description": "Cuántos eligieron cada punto, del 1 al 5." }
  }
}
```

```
app/packages/
├── contract/src/
│   └── polls.ts                         touched   PollType, ResponseValue y PollResults
├── core/src/polls/
│   └── fits-type.ts                     sin cambios: el feedback ya cae en la regla de la word cloud
└── database/src/
    └── schema.ts                        touched   "feedback" en el enum de polls.type
app/packages/database/migrations/        sin migración nueva
```

## 2 PATCH /polls/:id · la respuesta del alumno

### 2.1 Callstack · settled

```
 PATCH /api/polls/:id                                                       [[app/apps/api/src/handlers/polls.ts#PollsHandlers.vote]]
-given { myResponse: choice | scale | words }
+given { myResponse: choice | scale | words | { pick, text? } }             ← la rama nueva decodifica en el contract
 │
 └─ Polls.vote(viewer, id, response)                                        [[app/packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts#Polls.vote]]
    ├─ when viewer.role is not student → NotStudent (403)
    ├─ findPoll(id) → PollNotFound (404)                                    [[app/packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts#findPoll]]
    ├─ visibleSession(sessions, poll.sessionId) → PollNotFound (404)        [[app/packages/core/src/sessions/visible-session.ts#visibleSession]]
    ├─ when poll.status is not active → PollNotActive (409)
-   ├─ fitsPoll(poll, response) → InvalidResponse (400)                     [[app/packages/core/src/polls/tally.ts#fitsPoll]]
+   ├─ fitsPoll(poll, response) → InvalidResponse (400)    ← feedback acepta solo { pick }   [[app/packages/core/src/polls/tally.ts#fitsPoll]]
+   ├─ value = response.text is "" ? { pick } : response    ← saca el texto vacío
    ├─ crypto.randomULID                                                     id nuevo, solo lo usa el primer insert
-   ├─ responses.upsert({ id, pollId, userId, value: response }, target (pollId, userId))
+   ├─ responses.upsert({ id, pollId, userId, value }, target (pollId, userId))   ← reemplaza value y conserva el id
    ├─ classroom.notify(poll.sessionId, "polls")                            [[app/packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts#notifyPolls]]
    ├─ changelog.drop({ type: "poll-opened", entityId: poll.id })
    └─ forStudent(viewer, [poll])                                           [[app/packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts#forStudent]]
       ├─ responses.list(where userId, pollId)                               myResponse
-      ├─ shown = polls closed or answered
+      ├─ shown = polls not feedback and (closed or answered)  ← el feedback nunca entra
       ├─ responses.counts(shown)
       └─ Poll { …, myResponse, results: shown ? tally(…) : null }           feedback: results null
```

`GET /api/polls` llega a `forStudent` por `Polls.listForStudent` con las encuestas de la sesión, así que el inicio, el aula y las cerradas del alumno reciben el feedback con `results: null` por el mismo cambio. La regla: el alumno manda un punto y quizás un texto, la API lo acepta solo en una encuesta de feedback activa, guarda el texto tal como vino salvo que esté vacío, y nunca le devuelve resultados de un feedback.

### 2.2 Interfaces y module list · settled

```json
{
  "title": "PATCH /api/polls/:id",
  "$comment": "exists",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "input": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "myResponse": { "$ref": "kurasu.md#1.2/ResponseValue", "$comment": "changed: gana la rama feedback" }
      },
      "required": ["myResponse"]
    },
    "output": {
      "title": "Poll",
      "$comment": "exists",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "results": { "type": ["object", "null"], "$comment": "changed", "description": "Siempre null en una encuesta de feedback." }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

```
app/packages/core/src/polls/
├── polls.ts                             touched   texto vacío en vote; el feedback fuera de shown en forStudent
└── tally.ts                             touched   rama feedback en fitsPoll
app/apps/api/src/handlers/
└── polls.ts                             sin cambios: pasa myResponse tal como llega
```

### 2.3 Comportamiento crítico · settled

El texto vacío se saca en `Polls.vote`, después de `fitsPoll` y antes del `upsert`, y no en el schema del contract. Así el contract sigue describiendo lo que viaja, como las otras ramas, y la regla "vacío o ausente se guarda igual" vive en un solo lugar. El texto con espacios se guarda con sus espacios: el diseño pide no recortar.

Los resultados del alumno se niegan en `forStudent` y no en `tally`: `tally` sigue contando el feedback para el profe (3), y el alumno no ve resultados porque su encuesta nunca entra en `shown`. Como `counts` recibe solo `shown`, la query de conteos tampoco lee respuestas de feedback para el alumno.

## 3 GET /admin/polls · el resumen del profe

### 3.1 Callstack · settled

```
 GET /api/admin/polls?sessionId=                                            [[app/apps/api/src/handlers/polls.ts#AdminPollsHandlers.list]]

    return '\n'.join(js)

content.text:
Dibujé todo el program design en fast track en **http://localhost:5191**. Solo queda abierta la rama 4, con dos preguntas. El registro en texto está en `.scratch/feedback-de-sesion/program-design/kurasu.md`.

Las ramas 1, 2, 3, 5 y 6 quedaron settled. Cada una sale del design, de los prototipos o de cómo funciona el código hoy, y cada hoja dice de dónde viene:

- **1, el tipo feedback:** el contract suma `feedback` a `PollType`, la rama `{ pick, text? }` a `ResponseValue` y cinco conteos a `PollResults`. No hace falta migración, porque la columna `polls.type` es `text` sin `CHECK`.
- **2, la respuesta del alumno:** `fitsPoll` acepta en un feedback solo valores con `pick`. `Polls.vote` saca el texto vacío y `forStudent` deja el feedback afuera de los resultados, así que vuelve con `results: null`.

content.text:
`forStudent` y `forTeacher` no son servicios ni se exportan. Son dos funciones locales que `Polls.layer` define adentro de su `Effect.gen` (`app/packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts:100` y `:124`), así que usan el `ResponsesStore` que el layer ya obtuvo. Cada una convierte las encuestas guardadas (`StoredPoll`) en lo que ve un lado:

- **`forStudent(viewer, polls)`:** lee las respuestas del alumno para esas encuestas y con eso arma `myResponse`. Después arma `shown`, la lista de encuestas cerradas o ya respondidas, cuenta solo esas y devuelve `Poll`. `results` es `tally(…)` para las que están en `shown` y `null` para el resto. La llaman `listForStudent` (`GET /api/polls`) y `vote`, que la usa para devolver la encuesta recién votada.
- **`forTeacher(polls)`:** cuenta todas las encuestas y devuelve `AdminPoll`, siempre con `results`. La llaman `listForTeacher` (`GET /api/admin/polls`) y `update` (`PATCH /api/admin/polls/:id`). `create` no la usa: una encuesta nueva no tiene respuestas, así que usa `tally(poll, noResponses)`.

Por eso el cambio de la rama 2 va en `forStudent`: es el único lugar que decide qué ve el alumno, y lo usan tanto la lista como el voto. Dejé esta explicación como nota en la parte 2.1 del canvas, debajo de la prosa del callstack.

`changing` separa los dos estados que puede tener un alumno que ya respondió:

- **`false`:** la tarjeta muestra el estado de gracias (`FeedbackAnswer`) con "Cambiar mi respuesta".
- **`true`:** muestra el formulario con lo que el alumno mandó, el botón "Modificar feedback" y "Cancelar".

`poll.myResponse` solo dice si el alumno respondió; no alcanza para que "Cambiar mi respuesta" abra el formulario sin perder la respuesta guardada. Por eso hace falta un estado local que diga "estoy editando". Un envío exitoso o "Cancelar" lo vuelven a `false`. Si el alumno todavía no respondió, `changing` no interviene: con `myResponse == null` siempre se ve el formulario.

`VoteForm` ya tiene el mismo estado para "Cambiar mi voto" (`VoteForm.tsx:23`), y `FeedbackForm` sigue ese patrón. Si el nombre confunde, puede llamarse `editing`.

Uní las ramas 3 y 4 en una sola: **"3 GET /admin/polls · lo que ve el profe"**. Las dos partían del mismo endpoint y las dos se arman en `forTeacher`, así que ahora tienen un solo callstack, una sola lista de archivos y el comportamiento crítico de los conteos.

- **Rama 3, el callstack:** `counts` agrupa el feedback por `pick` y sin el texto. `feedbackOf` trae, en una sola query, las respuestas de todas las encuestas de feedback con el nombre y el avatar. `tally` arma las cinco barras y las encuestas de feedback llevan además `responses`.
- **Ramas renumeradas:** la tarjeta del alumno pasó a ser la 4, la del profe la 5 y Standards la 6. En el canvas las corrí una columna a la izquierda y les cambié el número en los títulos y en las etiquetas de cada parte.
- **Árbol y registro:** el árbol de arriba del canvas y `program-design/kurasu.md` ya tienen la nueva numeración, y la unión quedó anotada en "Decisiones de esta etapa".

Las seis ramas están settled. El paso que sigue es el cierre de program design: comparar el árbol con el design y con la nota `feedback-de-sesion.md`, y proponerte lo que hay que corregir en los docs. Hay al menos dos cosas que la nota ya no describe bien:
- **La lista del profe:** en el program design la lista viaja dentro de `AdminPoll`, sin endpoint propio.
- **La query de conteos:** ahora agrupa el feedback por `pick`.

¿Arranco con ese cierre?

# Test design with canvas

`test-design` and the skills it loads keep their procedure: roots, branches, classifications, partitions, matrices, facts, dropped rows, recording and ending.

When the user asks for a fast track, or fast track is already on in the session, load mahou:fast-track after mahou:canvas and before starting, unless it is already in context. It changes some of this skill's engagement rules.

The document is `canvas/test-design.tldr.json` in the change's scratch folder. The record stays `test-design/<repo>.md`; write a tree's change into it whenever the canvas changes, and draw the canvas from it.

## Roots on a map of the system

The candidate roots go on the canvas as a map of the system, under a title naming the change and the order the trees are worked in.

- **Each tree is an `area`**, labelled with its letter, its repository or deployable, and what it is to the rest of the system, such as `B <service>/: what a client calls`. Lay the areas out in the order work flows through them, whoever starts it on the left; put the tree that every other one imports along the bottom.
- **Each candidate root is a blue card** inside its tree's area. Its first line is an empty checkbox, `☐`, for the user to tick, then the root's id and its entry point; its second line is `e.g. <scenario>`, one or two scenarios through that entry point, an error case among them.
- **A candidate that is not a root is a grey dashed card** with the reason, such as a piece that runs only inside another entry point, or a migration, checked by one manual row.
- **Arrows join the cards that hand work to each other**, each labelled with the action one card asks of the other, such as `create` or `start`.

Tell the user to tick or cross out cards with sticky notes or by voice.

## Each branch is a classification tree

Each branch is an `area` labelled `<id> <root> · <status>`, inside its tree's area. Branches stack down their tree's area, and the trees sit side by side.

Draw every branch of a tree at once, each one whole: its root, classifications, partitions and matrix, labelled `proposed`. This replaces `test-design`'s one level and one branch at a time. A branch, and everything on it, stays `proposed` until the user approves it. Open the next tree once the user has approved every branch of the one before.

Draw each branch with `canvas`'s `classificationTree`, which lays out the root, the classifications, the partitions and the matrix. Keep each branch's spec as data in a script in the canvas folder. When a branch changes, such as a row turned manual or a partition added, call the helper again with the same name.

- **The root is a blue box** at the top, with the entry point and what it is given.
- **Each classification is a violet box** under the root, joined to it by a line with no arrowheads.
- **Each partition is a green box** under its classification, joined the same way, with a short label.
- **The matrix goes under the tree.** On the left, a narrow `★` column sits before `row · what the test does`, separated from it by a vertical dotted grey line; on the right, the header reads `expected · kind · setup`. Header labels are grey. Each row is one line: `★` in the first column when `isNew: true` and blank when the test already exists in the suite, its id and summary next to it, a filled dot under the centre of each partition it picks, and its expected outcome, kind and setup on the right. Dotted grey lines run between the rows and down each partition's column.
- **A row run by hand is orange**, its `★`, its text and its dots, whether it is `test + manual` or `manual`. Its expected outcome adds what the check observes by hand.
- **Dropped rows and deleted tests get grey lines under the matrix**, `Dropped: <reason>` and `Deleted: <test and reason>`. When either list is empty, nothing is drawn for it.
- **A branch with one row** draws its root and that row, with no classifications.

## Questions

A question goes inside the branch it is about, beside the classification, partition or row it discusses. A question about a root goes beside its card on the map. The branch's Agent note goes under the questions.

- **A question is a card with a violet border and no fill**, titled `❓ Q<n> · <title>`, then the body, which gives the situation and ends with the question. The card has no fill so it differs from the filled violet classification boxes.
- **Follow-ups stay inside the base question's card**, one at a time, until the question closes. The card holds, top to bottom: the base question, a summary box, one Agent note, and the current follow-up as a card of its own.
- **The summary box**, a solid grey rectangle labelled `Summary · Q<n> so far`, holds what the question has settled. Rewrite it each round; never add a line per answer.
- **When the question closes**, delete the card, redraw the branch with what it settled, and update the record.

## Messages from the agent

Everything you would say in the chat goes on the canvas, as an Agent note: a grey dashed rectangle labelled `Agent`, in the branch, tree or question it is about. One note at the top of the canvas says how to read the drawing and lists the implementation tasks the trees surfaced. Keep one Agent note per place and replace its text each round.

Follow the wiki indexes to the testing entries for the runners the repositories use, and read each repository's own testing conventions where the project keeps them, usually its `CLAUDE.md`: they decide the test level and the naming rule the rows follow.

# Test design

This skill applies the Classification Tree Method. Decompose a test object into the aspects that influence its behaviour, the classifications. Split each classification into disjoint classes, the partitions. A test case is a combination that picks one class per classification. Every question at every level is about what varies, how it is partitioned, and which combinations matter.

Takes a design the user has settled and produces, per repository, a tree whose leaves are the test cases and manual validations that prove the change, plus the combination matrix each branch resolves into. The matrix is built before any code exists so that whoever implements the change receives it as input. When the design tree is not at hand, the notes that record the design carry the decisions.

## How the tree is built

The user and the skill build each tree together, level by level: roots, then for one branch at a time its classifications, its partitions and its matrix. Every candidate comes from something already decided: a design leaf, a note's section, a fact read from the code. The skill shows the candidate for confirmation. The user confirms, cuts, merges or adds, and the next level opens on that answer.

The tree uses `design-tree`'s marks: `pending`, `open`, `settled`. Show the whole tree when the roots are confirmed, when a branch settles and at the end; otherwise show only the branch being worked. Row ids carry a letter per tree in the order the trees are worked and a running number across that tree: `A1`, `A2`, `B1`. A row can then be named from anywhere later.

## Roots

One tree per repository the change touches, worked from the repository the others depend on outward: the one that owns the data first, then the ones that consume it, then the one a person uses. When the order is not evident from the design, ask.

- On a service, a root is an entry point whose behaviour the change touches: an endpoint, a job, an event handler, a command, any way into the code. List the candidates from the design and, when code exists, from the diff, with what the change does in each, and let the user drop the ones the change does not reach. An entry point the change only crosses without altering its outcome is not a root; say why when the user asks.
  - A data migration has no root and no classification of its own. The other rows assume it ran. One manual row, outside the classifications, checks that its upgrade and its downgrade work.
  - A piece that runs only inside another entry point, such as a processor that executes during a read, is a classification of that entry point's branch, not a root.
- On a user-facing surface, a root is a main flow the change touches, including returning to a screen the user already completed when the change stores something there. The tree for such a surface covers each state a screen can show and each action that moves between them, so it is more exhaustive than a service's.
- On a user-facing surface, each placement of a flow, such as the same dialog opened from two parts of a page, is its own root. Each placement gets rows for every state and action the other placements cover.
- On a service, when two roots reach the same code the change adds, read the code to find which root reaches the added code on the usual path, and let the user confirm. The usual root carries the full matrix. The other root's branch covers only what that root's path adds, such as the states the root starts from. The branch title states that scope. Under that branch, list each classification the usual root already covers, with the rows that cover the classification, so none is hidden.

## Working a branch

Open one branch at a time, each on the approval of the previous.

1. **Classifications.** Read the existing test suite for the root's entry point, then derive the classifications from the design leaves that bear on the root, the change itself, and the cases the existing suite covers. Anything that influences the outcome is a candidate: the input the entry point receives, the state it starts from, the configuration it reads, the responses of the systems it calls, the actor and how the actor arrives, and the outcome itself when the outcome branches. Show each classification with the design leaf or existing behaviour it comes from. Rules the user applies and the skill proposes when it sees them:
   - Two classifications whose partitions determine each other are one classification. If every partition of the first fixes the partition of the second, merge them and carry the expectation on the partition.
   - A classification with one interesting partition scopes the branch instead of staying a classification when no existing test in the root's suite exercises the other partitions. State the scope in the branch title.
2. **Partitions.** One list per classification, each partition with its expected effect when the design fixes it. Two partitions that the code treats identically are one partition. When every input takes the code down the same path, the root is one row. A partition the design does not decide is asked, not filled in.
3. **Matrix.** One row per case that belongs to the entry point, including the cases the existing test suite already covers and the cases the change adds. Never drop a row because an existing test already covers it. A row picks one partition per classification. Every partition appears in at least one row, and the pairs of partitions that interact appear together. Columns: a narrow `★` column (`★` when the row is a new test added by the change, blank when the test already exists in the suite, whether kept as is or updated to match the row), the row id, a one-sentence summary of what the test does (not the test's function name), one column per classification, the expected outcome, the kind (`test` for an automated test through the entry point at the level the repository's conventions name, `manual` for a validation by hand against the running system, or both), and the setup column. Some rows need environment preparation: a seeded record, a configuration, a variant of an input. The setup column names that preparation and never includes test names. The skill builds the matrix and proposes the manual picks; the user adjusts rows and settles the picks.

Pick the manual checks from the test rows: a picked row's kind becomes `test + manual`, and its expected outcome adds what the check observes by hand. On a service they always include the most common flows and the most common error cases. A row is `manual` alone only when no automated test can check it. Schema rejections are not manual picks. On a surface whose repository has no test runner, every row is manual; whether it has one is a fact read from the repository, surfaced when the tree for it opens.

## Facts

The design is settled, so read the code whenever a partition, an expectation or a root depends on how the code behaves, without waiting to be asked. Before stating the state a root's rows start from, trace the entry point's call order up to the code the change adds: what runs before it and what is created after it. A starting state taken from the design alone is a guess. Surface every fact read this way in the level it affects; never apply one silently. When a fact contradicts a decision already settled, say so in the first sentence. A row whose expectation the code cannot meet is either corrected or becomes an implementation task; the user decides which, and record the task under the branch so the implementation receives it.

## Dropping rows and deleting existing tests

A row is dropped, never silently, when no realistic input reaches it. Examples of the kind of reason, not a list: two systems sharing the same schema cannot produce a validation error between them; a malformed response from another of our services is a programming error, unless the design makes one side validate the response's shape; input that the request type cannot carry, such as a field the request does not declare, never reaches the code; a value that only a hidden record carries cannot appear in a response; a state the flow cannot re-enter cannot be observed. State the reason in one line under the branch (`Dropped: <reason>`), so the row is not proposed again.

When the change alters or removes behaviour so an existing test in the suite no longer applies and is not updated as a row in the matrix, list it in one line under the branch (`Deleted: <test and reason>`). When no existing test is deleted, omit the line.

## Recording the design back

Questioning a tree settles more than tests: a member the design missed, a mechanism renamed mid-round, a gap the partitions exposed. Collect every amendment the trees produced, from what was read during the work; when the set is incomplete, say so. The user settles each one: amend the note, or carry it as an open decision.

Then run mahou:write-documentation once, handing it every settled amendment together, so it weighs how the changes affect the whole documentation rather than only the pieces the trees touched. An amendment landed during test-design follows the recording discipline the design itself followed: the text is shown before it lands, and unsloped with the note it joins.

## Ending

When every tree is settled, show them together with, per tree, the row range, the count of test rows and the manual picks, and list the implementation tasks the trees surfaced. Write each settled tree with its matrix to the change's scratch folder, at `test-design/<repo>.md`, so the trees survive the session. mahou:implement takes the trees as input; mahou:validate runs the manual rows.

Then check the scratch folder as mahou:basics says under Status.

## What this skill is not

It does not write tests and does not run anything. It does not propose a case the design does not imply.

# Test design in kurasu

- Automated tests are integration tests only, in the API and the web.
- A manual check is a web test row marked `test + manual`. Claude runs each one with agent-browser against the local stack. Every web branch has at least one. Pick the common cases, common errors included, such as a login with a user who has access and one who does not. Leave rare cases as tests only.
- API branches carry manual checks too: their most common rows, common errors included, marked `test + manual`. Claude runs each one against the local stack with HTTP requests, and checks the response and the state it leaves (the lists it changes, the mails the local binding writes). Leave rare cases as tests only.
- Checks that need production, such as the domain, real mail or hibernation, go in their own tree. Claude and the user run them by hand after the site launches on Cloudflare. They are not part of the design for the first implementation.

def status(branch):
    return "open" if any(q["branch"] == branch["key"] for q in QUESTIONS) else "settled"


def span(branch):
    ids = [r["id"] for r in branch["rows"]]
    return f"{ids[0]}–{ids[-1]}" if len(ids) > 1 else ids[0]


# ---------------- record
def ascii_tree(branch):
    lines = [branch["root"]]
    cls = branch["classifications"]
    for i, c in enumerate(cls):
        last = i == len(cls) - 1
        lines.append(("└─ " if last else "├─ ") + c["name"])
        for j, (_, label) in enumerate(c["partitions"]):
            lines.append(("   " if last else "│  ") + ("└─ " if j == len(c["partitions"]) - 1 else "├─ ") + label)
    return "\n".join(lines)


def table(branch):
    cls = branch["classifications"]
    head = ["★", "Fila", "Qué hace el test", *[c["name"] for c in cls], "Esperado", "Kind", "Setup"]
    out = ["| " + " | ".join(head) + " |", "|" + "---|" * len(head)]
    for r in branch["rows"]:
        picks = []
        for c, key in zip(cls, r["picks"]):
            picks.append("–" if key is None else dict(c["partitions"])[key])
        cells = ["★" if r["isNew"] else "", r["id"], r["summary"], *picks, r["expected"], r["kind"], r["setup"] or "–"]
        out.append("| " + " | ".join(cells) + " |")
    return "\n".join(out)

content.text:
Dejé la exploración a la derecha del canvas, debajo del título "Exploración · otras formas de leer las ramas". Los árboles y las matrices no los toqué. Son cuatro vistas de dos ramas: A#1, la respuesta del alumno, y la parte de feedback de B#1, la card del inicio.

1. **A#1 como el camino del pedido.** Es un flujo con los controles en el orden en que corren, y cada salida lleva las filas que la prueban. Se ve qué frena el pedido primero y por qué el feedback no necesita filas propias de rol o de encuesta oculta. No muestra las columnas de la matriz. Sirve para las ramas de la API.
2. **B#1 como estados de la tarjeta.** Es el mismo diagrama de estados del design, con la fila que prueba cada flecha. Un estado o una flecha sin fila es un test que falta. No muestra qué se verifica dentro de cada estado. Sirve para las ramas de pantalla.
3. **A#1 como grilla tipo × resultado.** Tiene dos ejes y cada celda dice qué filas la cubren. Se ve de un vistazo que el feedback tiene una fila por cada resultado que ya tenían los otros tipos. No muestra las clasificaciones menores, como el texto o la respuesta previa.
4. **A#1 como lista de lo nuevo.** Muestra solo las filas que agrega el cambio, agrupadas en "guarda" y "rechaza", una por línea. Es la más corta de leer, pero para revisar que no falte nada hay que volver a la matriz.

Una combinación posible: la 1 para las ramas de la API y la 2 para las de pantalla, para entender la cobertura, más la 4 al final de cada árbol con la lista de lo que hay que escribir. La matriz quedaría en el registro como respaldo. ¿Cuál te sirve, o qué mezcla?

Rehice las ramas para que tengan solo las clasificaciones que el cambio afecta. El canvas y `test-design/kurasu.md` pasan de 105 filas a 39.

- **Qué quedó en cada rama:** las clasificaciones que el feedback mueve y las filas que el cambio agrega o actualiza.
  - En A#1: el valor (`pick`), el texto, si la encuesta está activa o cerrada, y la respuesta previa.
  - En A#3 solo queda si el alumno respondió, porque activa o cerrada se tratan igual y no hace falta separarlas.
- **Qué salió:** las clasificaciones que el feedback no toca, como el rol, la encuesta borrada u oculta, choice, scale y words, o editar y borrar del profe. Los tests que ya existen y no cambian aparecen en gris, como una sola línea, "Sin cambios en la suite: …", debajo de cada rama. Así se ve qué sigue cubierto sin dibujar sus filas.
- **Las ramas que comparten código cubren solo lo suyo.** B#1, la card del inicio, tiene la matriz completa de `FeedbackForm`. B#2, el aula, prueba solo lo que agrega ese lugar: las activas, Cerradas, el cierre mientras el alumno responde y el badge.
- **Pruebas a mano:** siguen en naranja. Son 14 entre los dos árboles.

Guardé la versión anterior de las ramas en `canvas/td-spec-full.py`, por si querés comparar.

Siguen abiertas Q1 (B#5), Q2 (B#1) y Q3 (B#4), a la derecha de cada rama.

content.text:
Separé las variantes en las dos clasificaciones que marcaste, y A#1 y A#2 quedaron redibujadas en el canvas.

**A#1, "Texto"**, que antes juntaba todo en "con texto", ahora tiene siete particiones, cada una con su fila:
- sin la clave
- vacío
- solo espacios
- común
- con espacios alrededor: se guarda sin recortar
- largo, de 5000 caracteres: se guarda entero, porque no tiene tope
- con saltos de línea y emojis: se guarda tal cual

"Valor" también quedó separado en `pick` 0, 6 y 2.5, cada uno con su fila. El texto no se combina con esos valores, porque el schema rechaza `pick` antes de mirarlo.

**A#2, "Respuestas"**, ahora tiene cuatro particiones:
- **Ninguna:** cinco ceros y `responses: []`.
- **Una:** una sola barra en 1.
- **Puntos distintos, con 1 y 5:** el 1 cae en la primera barra y el 5 en la última, en orden por id, y la que no tiene texto no lleva `text`.
- **Varias en el mismo punto:** tres en el 4 con textos distintos, que suman una sola barra de 3.

Además sumé "Texto de cada una" (todas con texto o alguna sin texto), y la edición pasó a cambiar del 1 al 5.

Al separar estas variantes apareció **Q4**, al lado de A#1: ¿un texto de solo espacios cuenta como vacío? El design dice "sin recortar", así que hoy se guardaría tal cual y la hoja del profe mostraría una fila en blanco en vez de "Sin comentario.". Las opciones son guardarlo así, o que la API saque la clave cuando el texto sin espacios queda vacío y que la web no lo mande. En los dos casos, un texto con contenido conserva sus espacios.

Los dos árboles suman ahora 72 filas. Las renumeré de forma correlativa dentro de cada árbol, así que los números cambiaron: A1–A35 y B1–B37. Siguen abiertas Q1 (B#5), Q2 (B#1), Q3 (B#4) y Q4 (A#1).

Turns a session's friction into something reusable. The plugin grows this way, by keeping the corrections the user just made by hand instead of designing a pipeline upfront.

## Modes

Pick the mode from what the user asks.

- **Discovery.** Follow `references/discover.md` when the user asks for nothing specific, or asks what the session, or a part of it, has to teach.
- **Directed.** Follow `references/directed.md` when the user names what to build.
- **Mixed.** When the user names some items and also asks what else there is, work the named items as directed and run discovery over the part of the session the ask points at.

Before starting, tell the user which mode you are following. For a mixed ask, list the items you work as directed and the part of the session discovery covers. Every mode continues with Drafting once there is an item to draft.

## Fidelity

Anything produced here reproduces the patterns the session established exactly. The formats, the visualizations, the wording of a rule, the order of steps, and every correction the user made along the way are the specification. Do not adapt them, improve them, or generalize them into something the session did not do.

Examples inside a skill or wiki entry are generic. They carry the shape the session used, with placeholders in place of the session's tickets, repositories and field names. A code example in a wiki entry names its components, hooks, endpoints and fields after a generic resource, such as `ResourceActionButton` or `useResourceAction`, never after the session's feature.

## Drafting

1. **Classify and scope each item before drafting it.** Process becomes a skill, new or iterated. Work a skill should hand to a subagent becomes an agent. Knowledge about a tool or technology becomes a wiki entry. A decision the user repeated for this project becomes a standing rule in a local file. A rule every change to this project respects, about how the product behaves or how the system is built, becomes a line in the project's invariants note. Global means useful in any project; local means true only for this one. Restate the job the item does, which kind it is and where it lands. Read the skill, entry or index it would land in to check it is not already there; if it already says this, the finding becomes an iteration on whatever failed to read it. Draft only once the user confirms the shape.

2. **Draft every item in one reply**, ordered by confidence then by impact, each under its own heading, with the file it lands in. For a new skill, agent, wiki entry, design type or program design representation, give the full text; for an iteration, the old and new text. Before showing the drafts, write them to the change's scratch folder, per the convention in mahou:basics, and run `superpowers:unslop` over them. The user approves, corrects or drops each item separately; do not ask for a single approve-everything answer, though the user may give one.

   - A new skill: the full draft, following the new skill checklist.
   - A skill iteration: the exact change and the reason it is needed.
   - An agent: the full draft, plus the change to the skill that dispatches it.
   - A wiki entry: the draft plus its line in the index at the right level.
   - A local file: the draft and which skill it changes.

3. **Write each approved item** to its place. Leave everything uncommitted.

## Where things land

| Finding | Lands as |
|---|---|
| Reusable process | `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in the plugin |
| Work a skill should hand to a subagent | `agents/<name>.md` in the plugin, dispatched by the skill that needs it |
| Knowledge about a tool or technology | `skills/wiki/references/<topic>/<entry>.md`, plus its line in that folder's `INDEX.md` |
| A design type that generalizes beyond the session it came from | `skills/design/references/types/<type>.md`, plus its row in the types table of mahou:design. A type specific to one change stays out |
| A program design representation that generalizes beyond the session it came from | `skills/program-design/references/representations/<form>.md`, plus its row in the representations table of mahou:program-design. A form specific to one change stays out |
| A rule or fact true only for this project | `.mahou/<skill>.md`, or `.mahou/wiki/` with the same index-per-level shape as the global store |
| A rule every change to this project respects | A line in the project's invariants note, in the section for its kind, linking the note that explains it when one does |

## New skill checklist

- A descriptive name. The magic vocabulary stays in mahou:basics and the README.
- One job. Two jobs means proposing two skills.
- A description precise enough to load when intended, and to let mahou:guide match goals to it. Descriptions that overlap an existing skill's are the main way routing degrades.
- First lines of the body: load mahou:basics, then read `.mahou/<skill>.md` if present.
- No decisions delegated to the agent. It maps the state and asks; the user settles. A draft that contains "choose the best option" or "decide whether" is not ready.
- Nothing committed as a side effect.

## Removing or replacing a skill

When an item replaces an existing skill, the replacement is not done until the old directory is removed and every reference to it is updated: the plugin README and every skill that names it. List those edits as part of the item.

## Committing

Propose, never commit. When the user accepts an item, write the files and stop. Version bumps belong to whatever commits the marketplace; never hand-edit a `plugin.json` version.

- On a service, when two roots reach the same code the change adds, read the code to find which root reaches the added code on the usual path, and let the user confirm. The usual root carries the full matrix. The other root's branch covers only what that root's path adds, such as the states the root starts from. The branch title states that scope. Under that branch, list each classification the usual root already covers, with the rows that cover the classification, so none is hidden.

## Working a branch

Open one branch at a time, each on the approval of the previous.

1. **Classifications.** Read the existing test suite for the root's entry point, then derive the classifications from the design leaves that bear on the root, the change itself, and the cases the existing suite covers. Anything that influences the outcome is a candidate: the input the entry point receives, the state it starts from, the configuration it reads, the responses of the systems it calls, the actor and how the actor arrives, and the outcome itself when the outcome branches. Show each classification with the design leaf or existing behaviour it comes from. Rules the user applies and the skill proposes when it sees them:
   - Two classifications whose partitions determine each other are one classification. If every partition of the first fixes the partition of the second, merge them and carry the expectation on the partition.
   - A classification with one interesting partition scopes the branch instead of staying a classification when no existing test in the root's suite exercises the other partitions. State the scope in the branch title.
2. **Partitions.** One list per classification, each partition with its expected effect when the design fixes it. Two partitions that the code treats identically are one partition. When every input takes the code down the same path, the root is one row. A partition the design does not decide is asked, not filled in.
3. **Matrix.** One row per case that belongs to the entry point, including the cases the existing test suite already covers and the cases the change adds. Never drop a row because an existing test already covers it. A row picks one partition per classification. Every partition appears in at least one row, and the pairs of partitions that interact appear together. Columns: a narrow `★` column (`★` when the row is a new test added by the change, blank when the test already exists in the suite, whether kept as is or updated to match the row), the row id, a one-sentence summary of what the test does (not the test's function name), one column per classification, the expected outcome, the kind (`test` for an automated test through the entry point at the level the repository's conventions name, `manual` for a validation by hand against the running system, or both), and the setup column. Some rows need environment preparation: a seeded record, a configuration, a variant of an input. The setup column names that preparation and never includes test names. The skill builds the matrix and proposes the manual picks; the user adjusts rows and settles the picks.

Pick the manual checks from the test rows: a picked row's kind becomes `test + manual`, and its expected outcome adds what the check observes by hand. On a service they always include the most common flows and the most common error cases. A row is `manual` alone only when no automated test can check it. Schema rejections are not manual picks. On a surface whose repository has no test runner, every row is manual; whether it has one is a fact read from the repository, surfaced when the tree for it opens.

## Facts

The design is settled, so read the code whenever a partition, an expectation or a root depends on how the code behaves, without waiting to be asked. Before stating the state a root's rows start from, trace the entry point's call order up to the code the change adds: what runs before it and what is created after it. A starting state taken from the design alone is a guess. Surface every fact read this way in the level it affects; never apply one silently. When a fact contradicts a decision already settled, say so in the first sentence. A row whose expectation the code cannot meet is either corrected or becomes an implementation task; the user decides which, and record the task under the branch so the implementation receives it.

## Dropping rows and deleting existing tests

A row is dropped, never silently, when no realistic input reaches it. Examples of the kind of reason, not a list: two systems sharing the same schema cannot produce a validation error between them; a malformed response from another of our services is a programming error, unless the design makes one side validate the response's shape; input that the request type cannot carry, such as a field the request does not declare, never reaches the code; a value that only a hidden record carries cannot appear in a response; a state the flow cannot re-enter cannot be observed. State the reason in one line under the branch (`Dropped: <reason>`), so the row is not proposed again.

When the change alters or removes behaviour so an existing test in the suite no longer applies and is not updated as a row in the matrix, list it in one line under the branch (`Deleted: <test and reason>`). When no existing test is deleted, omit the line.

## Recording the design back

Questioning a tree settles more than tests: a member the design missed, a mechanism renamed mid-round, a gap the partitions exposed. Collect every amendment the trees produced, from what was read during the work; when the set is incomplete, say so. The user settles each one: amend the note, or carry it as an open decision.

## Each branch is a classification tree

Each branch is an `area` labelled `<id> <root> · <status>`, inside its tree's area. Branches stack down their tree's area, and the trees sit side by side.

Draw every branch of a tree at once, each one whole: its root, classifications, partitions and matrix, labelled `proposed`. This replaces `test-design`'s one level and one branch at a time. A branch, and everything on it, stays `proposed` until the user approves it. Open the next tree once the user has approved every branch of the one before.

Draw each branch with `canvas`'s `classificationTree`, which lays out the root, the classifications, the partitions and the matrix. Keep each branch's spec as data in a script in the canvas folder. When a branch changes, such as a row turned manual or a partition added, call the helper again with the same name.

- **The root is a blue box** at the top, with the entry point and what it is given.
- **Each classification is a violet box** under the root, joined to it by a line with no arrowheads.
- **Each partition is a green box** under its classification, joined the same way, with a short label.
- **The matrix goes under the tree.** On the left, a narrow `★` column sits before `row · what the test does`, separated from it by a vertical dotted grey line; on the right, the header reads `expected · kind · setup`. Header labels are grey. Each row is one line: `★` in the first column when `isNew: true` and blank when the test already exists in the suite, its id and summary next to it, a filled dot under the centre of each partition it picks, and its expected outcome, kind and setup on the right. Dotted grey lines run between the rows and down each partition's column.
- **A row run by hand is orange**, its `★`, its text and its dots, whether it is `test + manual` or `manual`. Its expected outcome adds what the check observes by hand.

content.text:
Uso el modo **mixto**. Los cambios que le pediste al test design los trabajo como ítems dirigidos. El resto de la sesión lo recorro en modo descubrimiento, y de esa parte solo listo las fricciones, sin proponer nada. La primera parte de la sesión (explore, shape, design y el principio de program design) está compactada, así que las fricciones de ese tramo salen del resumen y puede faltar alguna.

## Todas las fricciones, en orden

**1. Estrellas a emojis, filas a barras (explore/design, resumen).** Corregiste dos veces cómo se ve el puntaje: primero estrellas y después filas de elección. Las dos veces terminó en lo que ya existía, los emojis y las barras de la escala. Reusar lo que el producto ya tiene apareció como corrección, no como paso del flujo.

**2. El reviewer de documentación no corrió solo.** `write-documentation` pide pasar el `documentation-reviewer` antes de mostrar el borrador, y lo salteé; lo pediste vos ("lo corramos"). La skill ya lo pide, así que lo que falló fue cumplirla, no la regla.

**3. Un diff de código dentro del program design.** Pediste ver un diff de la lógica de encuestas contra la de hoy "para entender cómo afecta". `program-design` prohíbe mostrar código en las partes, y no tiene un lugar para un boceto de código que sirva para entender y quede fuera del registro. Ese lugar lo improvisamos.

**4. El diff en la rama equivocada, dos veces.** "Movelo a la rama donde te pregunté" lo leí como la rama de las preguntas abiertas, la 4, y vos te referías a la 2. Después lo dejé en la columna correcta pero afuera de la rama. Fueron errores míos al leer la referencia por voz.

**5. Notas del `code-snippet` amontonadas.** El mock de la skill de canvas les da 260 de ancho fijo. Intenté arreglarlo y auto-mode lo bloqueó por estar fuera del repo; al refrescar el canvas se veía bien. No quedó claro si es un problema del mock o del render.

**6. Un endpoint propio para la lista del profe.** En program design propuse `GET /api/admin/responses` y lo marqué como si siguiera de la wiki `api`. Vos lo cambiaste por meter la lista en `AdminPoll`, porque es "lo que ya hace" `forTeacher`. Esa propuesta abrió dos preguntas, Q1 y Q2, que desaparecieron con tu cambio. `program-design` pide buscar primero lo que el código ya resuelve; lo hice para las funciones, no para la forma del endpoint.

**7. Que la decisión se propague a todo.** Tuviste que preguntar si con Q3 había que actualizar las otras ramas. Fast track dice que una hoja corregida vuelve a ❔, pero no dice que una decisión que cambia una forma compartida obligue a revisar las ramas que la usan.

**8. Dos ramas para el mismo entry point.** Las ramas 3 y 4 eran ambas `GET /api/admin/polls`, y pediste unirlas. `program-design` define una rama por entry point; yo las separé por tema, el resumen por un lado y la lista por otro.

**9. `changing` → `isEditing`.** Pediste el prefijo `is` "como todas las variables booleanas". No está en el `AGENTS.md` global ni en la wiki `fence`, así que es una convención que hoy existe solo en la sesión.

**10. Test design: buscar otra forma de leerlo.** Las matrices se te hicieron difíciles de leer. Probamos cuatro vistas y después una quinta, y descartaste todas. No quedó ningún formato nuevo, pero sí la señal de que el problema era el volumen.

**11. Test design: solo lo que el cambio afecta.** Pediste quedarte con las clasificaciones que el cambio mueve. Eso choca con la regla de la skill: "una fila por cada caso del entry point, incluidos los que la suite ya cubre; nunca sacar una fila porque un test ya la cubre".

**12. Test design: lo que el cambio toca de lo existente.** Pediste tener en cuenta que agregar el feedback cambia cómo funcionan las otras encuestas. La skill no tiene un paso que pregunte qué código compartido toca el cambio y qué tests existentes lo cubren.

**13. Test design: separar las variantes que se discutieron.** Pediste no juntar el texto en "con texto" y abrir cada variante, y lo mismo con las respuestas en distintos puntos. La skill pide unir las particiones "que el código trata igual". Al separarlas apareció Q4, el texto en blanco, que cambió el design.

**14. Test design: no reescribir todo.** "No hace falta que reescribas todo entero cada vez." `test-design-with-canvas` ya dice que, cuando una rama cambia, se llama al helper otra vez con el mismo nombre; yo borraba el canvas y lo regeneraba entero. Es otra regla que existía y no seguí.

¿Coinciden con lo que recordás?

## Los cambios al test design (dirigidos)

**Estado actual.** El repo del plugin está en `main` y limpio. La copia en caché difiere solo en el formato del frontmatter. Lo que tocan los ítems:
- **`test-design/SKILL.md`:** "Working a branch", pasos 1 a 3, y "Dropping rows and deleting existing tests".
- **`test-design-with-canvas/SKILL.md`:** "Each branch is a classification tree".
- **Quienes leen las matrices:**
  - `implement`: pasa las filas tal cual, con su ★.
  - `implement-with-tdd`: el tester escribe los tests de las filas ★ y actualiza las filas sin ★.
  - `validate`: corre las filas manuales.
- **Archivo local:** este proyecto tiene `.mahou/test-design.md`.

Leo los ítems así:

- **A. Alcance por cambio.** Una rama tiene solo las clasificaciones que el cambio mueve y las filas que el cambio agrega o actualiza. Los tests que ya existen y no recorren nada de lo que cambia quedan en una línea bajo la rama: "Sin cambios en la suite: …". Reemplaza la regla de que la matriz lleva todos los casos del entry point.
- **B. Regresión del código compartido.** Antes de armar las ramas, se lista lo que el cambio toca de código que otros casos también recorren. Cada rama suma la clasificación que separa esos casos (acá, "Tipo") con los tests que ya existen como filas de regresión, sin ★. El registro y el canvas llevan una tabla "lo que el cambio toca" con su columna "filas que lo cubren".
- **C. Una partición por variante discutida.** Cada variante de un input que el design, la nota o la conversación nombraron es su propia partición, con su fila. No se une a otra aunque el código parezca tratarlas igual. Ajusta la regla de "el código las trata igual".
- **D. Cambios chicos sin redibujar todo.** Las ramas viven como datos en un solo archivo, el registro y el canvas se generan desde ahí, y un cambio redibuja solo la rama tocada, sin borrar el canvas. Es una iteración sobre la regla que ya existe en `test-design-with-canvas`.

Dejo afuera las exploraciones de formato (fricción 10), porque no quedó ninguna.

**Lo que los ítems dejan abierto:**

1. **Alcance.** ¿A, B y C van en el plugin, en `test-design`, o en el `.mahou/test-design.md` de este proyecto? ¿Y D, en `test-design-with-canvas` o en `canvas`?
2. **Las filas sin ★.** Con B, hay filas que ya existen y no cambian, como "cambia el voto de una escala", y filas que ya existen y se actualizan. Hoy `implement-with-tdd` actualiza toda fila sin ★. ¿Se distinguen con una marca o una columna, o se deja así?
3. **El borde de C.** ¿Una variante se abre aunque el código ya la trate igual que otra (por ejemplo, `pick` 0, 6 y 2.5, que el schema rechaza igual), o solo cuando el design o la conversación la nombraron?
4. **¿Se renumeran las filas?** Al abrir variantes renumeré todo el árbol, de A1 a A36. ¿Las filas se renumeran cuando cambia una rama, o conservan su id y las nuevas van al final?

Con eso redacto los cuatro ítems.

Every part rests on the code and follows the conventions, and every part is a representation of the code, never the code itself. No function bodies, no declarations in the language's syntax, no snippet that would compile. Some parts carry complex logic or solve a problem other code already solves, such as reading a standard format or running a well-known algorithm. ## Merging

The user may ask to merge parts of the tree that turn out to be one decision or one area.

### Questions

Two open questions that one answer would settle become one. The merged question keeps the lower number, its title names what both decide, and its body carries the context of both. Remove the other question's leaf and do not reuse its number. The merged question's leaf records the merge, for instance "❔ Q3 <what is undecided> (Q5 merged)". A merged question that waits on a lookup waits on every lookup the two had.

### Branches

A branch whose decisions another branch already settled folds into the receiving branch. Its settled leaves that the receiving branch does not hold yet move there, its open decisions become questions there, and the receiving branch goes back to open if it was settled. The folded branch stays in the tree as one line, marked "merged into <n>", with a leaf saying where its content went. Keeping it there leaves the numbers of the other branches unchanged.

Saqué las fricciones que no querías y apliqué tus comentarios a las demás. Quedan cuatro: la 3, la 7, la 9 y el test design, que junta la 11, la 12 y la 13 como un solo cambio.

## Fricciones que quedan

**3. El diff de código en program design.** Tenés razón, lo leí mal. `program-design` dice que una *parte* se representa sin código ("every part is a representation of the code, never the code itself"). No prohíbe que el usuario pida un boceto de código para ver el detalle de algo. El problema es que la skill no dice que se puede pedir ni dónde va: si entra en el registro, si queda al lado de la parte que detalla, y qué marca lo distingue de una parte. Hoy lo cubre la regla de "nunca código", y por eso yo lo traté como una excepción improvisada.

**7. Propagar una corrección a lo que depende de ella.** No es algo de fast track. `design-tree` dice qué pasa con la hoja corregida: vuelve a ❔. No dice que las ramas y las hojas que dependían de esa decisión también se revisen. Esa regla general hoy no está en ninguna skill. Con Q3 la tuviste que pedir vos.

**9. `changing` → `isEditing`.** Los booleanos llevan el prefijo `is`. No está en tu `AGENTS.md` global ni en la wiki `fence`, así que hoy es una convención que solo existe en esta sesión.

## Test design (dirigido)

Con tus comentarios, lo leo como **un solo cambio** en `test-design/SKILL.md`, en "Working a branch", paso 1:

> **Las clasificaciones salen de lo que el cambio afecta.** Una rama clasifica solo los inputs, estados y salidas que el cambio mueve, y no todo lo que influye en el entry point. Dos fuentes amplían esa lista. Primero, el código que el cambio toca y que otros casos también recorren: la rama suma la clasificación que separa esos casos (acá, "Tipo"), y los tests existentes que los recorren entran como filas de regresión. Segundo, las variantes que se discutieron en los pasos anteriores: cada una que el design, la nota, los prototipos o la conversación nombraron es su propia partición, con al menos una fila, así todo lo que se decidió queda probado.

**Lo que se mantiene:** la matriz sigue mostrando todos los tests del entry point que caen en esas clasificaciones, existan o no. El cambio solo achica la cantidad de variantes a probar, no saca filas porque ya existan.

**Los dos pasos que esto ajusta:**
- **"Una fila por cada caso del entry point"** pasa a ser "una fila por cada caso dentro de las clasificaciones de la rama". Los tests existentes que no recorren nada de lo que cambia se nombran en una línea bajo la rama.
- **"Dos particiones que el código trata igual son una"** queda con una excepción: una variante discutida en los pasos anteriores no se une con otra.

**Lo que queda abierto:**
1. **Dónde va.** ¿En el plugin, en `test-design`, o en el `.mahou/test-design.md` de este proyecto?
2. **Los tests existentes que no cambian.** Con este cambio, una rama tiene filas existentes de regresión. Hoy `implement-with-tdd` actualiza cualquier fila sin ★. ¿Se distingue "ya existe y no cambia" de "ya existe y se actualiza", o queda como está?
3. **La línea de los que quedan afuera.** ¿Los tests existentes que no recorren el cambio se nombran bajo la rama, como hice ("Sin cambios en la suite: …"), o no se mencionan?
4. **¿Las fricciones 3, 7 y 9 se trabajan también?** Si sí, ¿cuáles?

1. en el plugin
2. claro, hay que incluir regresiones; implement-with-tdd debería tener en cuenta eso también, si no cambia no hace falta tocarla (pero debería seguir pasando), si cambia hay que modificarlo
3. no hace falta incluirlos
4. 3 y 7 van a lplugin, 9 a la wiki local

For each repository, spawn two subagents from this session, a tester and an implementer, labelled `<repository>: tester` and `<repository>: implementer`. Both get the repository's full brief from `implement` and work in the same checkout, on the same branch. Neither spawns the other, and they never talk to each other directly. Every exchange passes through this session. The session relays each exchange between the tester and the implementer and records it in the repository's section of `implementation-status.md`. The session does not show an exchange to the user when the exchange arrives.

Neither subagent commits. That is the only change to the brief's repository rules.

## The rounds

1. **Red.** The tester writes the new tests for the repository's `★` `test` rows, updates any unstarred `test` rows whose expected outcome changed, and removes any tests listed under `Deleted:`. It runs the suite and confirms that each new or updated test fails because the behaviour is missing, not because the test is broken. When the tests cannot load before the code exists, it says how it checked the reason for the failure. It reports the row-to-test mapping, the files it changed and why each test fails.
2. **Green.** Relay the failing tests and the changed files to the implementer. It writes the code until the tests pass, then reports the linter and test output tail.
3. **Validate.** Relay the implementer's report to the tester. The tester runs the suite and checks the code against the design's rules and contracts, not only against the tests. It answers with an approval or with concrete feedback. Relay the feedback to the implementer and repeat 2 and 3 until the tester approves.

Rules for the rounds:

- The implementer does not edit test files. When it believes a test is wrong, it says so, and this session relays the claim to the tester.
- The tester does not edit the implementation.
- When either subagent finds a design ambiguity that changes the outcome, this session asks the user. Neither subagent decides it.

## Committing

Once the tester approves, this session commits the repository's changes with mahou:commit-changes, then continues with `implement`'s agentic review for that repository.
----

Every subagent gets the same brief, filled for its repository. Nothing in it is optional, and the brief leaves the subagent nothing to look up.

- **The change.** The design notes by path or URL, and a design summary in the brief itself: what changes, the shapes that cross systems, the rules the design settled, what is out of scope. Tell it to read the notes before touching code, with the reasoning effort the user named.
- **The tasks.** The ones assigned to its repository, each with what it requires in one or two sentences and the order to work them in. Without a tracker, the list comes from the test-design trees and the user.
- **The tests.** The matrix rows of the subagent's repository, verbatim, with each row's `★` mark, expected outcome and kind, plus any `Deleted:` lines under each branch, read from the change's scratch folder at `test-design/<repo>.md` when test-design wrote them there. On `test` rows (including `test + manual`), a `★` row is a new test the subagent writes, at the level the repository's conventions name and named after what the test proves; an unstarred row already exists in the suite and is kept as is or updated when the row's expected outcome changed; a test listed under `Deleted:` is removed from the suite. The rows carry ids for the matrix only: no row id, tracker id, or scratch path appears in a test name, comment, or docstring; the mapping stays in the scratch folder and out of the repository. The `manual` rows are for later; the subagent does not run them.
- **Repository rules.** Fetch and pull the default branch as mahou:changeset resolves it, create the branch the user named from it; stop and ask when the working tree is dirty or the repository sits on another branch with unpushed work. Follow the project's `CLAUDE.md`, `.mahou/basics.md` when present, the wiki entries for the technologies it touches, and the user's own coding style file. Where a wiki entry defines a component or library for what you are building, use it instead of writing a custom equivalent; on frontend screens, start from the wiki's frontend entries. The prototype settles how the change looks and behaves, not how it is coded. Keep changes minimal and consistent with the surrounding code. Run linters and the full relevant suites; everything must pass. Commit on the branch through mahou:commit-changes, and commit the groups it proposes without asking the user to confirm them; do not push, do not open a pull request. Do not touch other repositories. Avoid `rm -rf` when another way works, such as `rm -r` on a named path or leaving temporary files in `/tmp`, because a permission rule can turn `rm -rf` into a dialog that blocks the subagent until the user answers.
- **Tracker states**, only when the project tracks tasks: move each task to the tracker's in-progress state when it starts it and to its done state when its change is implemented, tested and committed, using the tool and the state names the project declares. The list stays current: work the tracker does not register becomes a new task, created and worked like the rest; a task that dissolves mid-work is closed with a line saying why. Each is named in the report. The tracker can be anything (Linear, Jira, Notion, GitHub issues, a beads database) and the brief names it concretely.
- **How to answer.** A report in the shape mahou:report gives: the branch, the commits, a summary per change, the row-to-test mapping, the linter and test output tail, and what it could not resolve. The report is the whole of the subagent's final message, because the session that collects the result reads only that message. A shorter message sent after the report replaces it. Every later instruction to the subagent repeats this. A design ambiguity that changes the outcome is a question back through the subagent's question channel, not a guess. The subagent applies a fix the user decided exactly as the user decided it. When the subagent thinks another fix fits better, it asks through the same channel instead of applying its own.

Knowledge about technologies and tools, their gotchas and their patterns, lives in mahou:wiki, indexed one level per folder so entries load on demand. Load it now and read its root indexes, global and local, so that you know which topics have entries when they come up in conversation. ## The project's docs

Projects mahou runs in keep their own documentation in a folder they own, usually `docs/`. How to find it and what its structure is made of live in mahou:docs, which every skill and agent that reads or writes documentation loads. Skills that do not touch documentation leave it alone.

## The project's invariants

Projects keep the rules that every change respects in an invariants note in their docs folder. The rules cover how the product behaves and how the system is built. # One hook per API operation, with the query options passed through

verified: 2026-10-18

Answers how screens reach an API through TanStack Query when several screens use the same operation: where the query key, the call and the invalidation live, and how a screen still tunes the query.

## Knowledge

- Write one hook per API operation, each in its own file, in the folder of the resource it touches: `useResources(filters)`, `useResource(id)`, `useCreateResource()`. Screens call these hooks and never call `useQuery` or `useMutation` directly.
- A query hook builds its key from a shared key factory and calls the typed API client. A mutation hook declares what it invalidates, or what it writes into the cache with `setQueryData`.
- Besides the operation's arguments, every hook takes an optional `options` with everything `useQuery` or `useMutation` accepts except `queryKey`, `queryFn` and `mutationFn`. Type `options` with the operation's result, its error union and, for a mutation, its input, such as `Omit<UseMutationOptions<Resource, ResourceError, CreateResourceInput>, 'mutationFn'>`.
- The hook writes its own settings first and spreads `options` on top, so a screen can set `enabled`, `select`, `refetchInterval` or callbacks. A screen's `onSuccess` runs after the hook's own invalidation, so it sees fresh data.
- The hook returns what `useQuery` or `useMutation` returns.

```ts
export const useCreateResource = (options?: Omit<UseMutationOptions<Resource, ResourceError, CreateResourceInput>, 'mutationFn'>) => {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient()

  return useMutation({
    ...options,
    mutationFn: (input) => runApi((client) => client.resources.create({ payload: input })),
    onSuccess: async (data, input, context) => {
      await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: resourceKeys.lists() })
      await options?.onSuccess?.(data, input, context)
    },
  })
}
```
